ICLR 2026 Test-Time Updates (TTU) Workshop
HIDRA: A BLAZINGFASTLM-HEADREPLACEMENT
Satyajit Kumar, Henry Ndubuaku
Cactus Compute
{satyajit, henry}@cactuscompute.com
ABSTRACT
The output projection (LMHead) in large language models scales linearly with
vocabulary size and constitutes a major portion of decoding cost, often at least
10% on sub-1B models which are often deployed on small consumer hardware.
We propose HiDRA (Hierarchical Decision Routing Architecture), a post-training
method that replaces the dense vocabulary projection with a hierarchical se-
quence of binary decisions, reducing the computational complexity fromO(V)
toO(logV)dot products per token. The hierarchy is constructed on top of an
existing model by hierarchically splitting the embedding space in half by a sin-
gle hyperplane. We prove that minimizing the error rate of a given hyperplane is
equivalent to a Linear Discriminant Analysis optimization problem. On Gemma
with WildChat completions, HiDRA achieves an8.04×practical CPU speedup
for the full output stage including routing, while reducing top-1 accuracy by4.2%
absolute at a moderate routing depth with beam search. More generally, different
depths provide a smooth spectrum of operating points, allowing practitioners to
select the desired balance between compute and model quality without retraining
the base model.
1 INTRODUCTION
In modern language models, the final projection layer (LMHead) computes logits
zk =h ⊤ek,
whereh∈R d is the hidden state and{ek}V
k=1 are token embeddings. This operation requires a dense
matrix multiplication of costO(V d)per decoding step, which scales linearly with vocabulary size.
This projection often dominates inference latency on edge devices, where CPU-based execution is
common, and large LMHead matrix multiplications can significantly impede sustained generation.
At the same time, the probability mass of the output distribution is typically concentrated on a small
fraction of the vocabulary. We aim to reduce the number of projections the model has to perform,
decreasing output-projection latency and alleviating sustained CPU load during decoding.
We propose HiDRA (Hierarchical Decision Routing Architecture), a replacement for the LMHead
that uses a binary decision tree over tokens. Each token is assigned a binary path of lengthL≈
log2 V. At inference time, the hidden state is routed through a sequence of hyperplane decisions
requiring onlyO(Ld)computation, followed by evaluating LMHead just on the candidate tokens at
the leaf. This reduces the effective computation fromO(V d)toO(Ld+ (V /2L)d).
We provide a theoretical analysis showing that this problem is aligned with the Fisher Linear Dis-
criminant, an existing optimization problem. This motivates the initialization for the decision vectors
that we use to construct the hyperplanes. This leads to stable routing and improved empirical per-
formance. A key property of the method is that the tree can be truncated at any depth, yielding a
continuous tradeoff between speed and accuracy without retraining or architectural changes.
2 RELATEDWORK
Large-vocabulary neural language models have long relied on hierarchical output layers to reduce
the cost of the softmax projection. Early work introduced hierarchical softmax for neural language
1
ICLR 2026 Test-Time Updates (TTU) Workshop
modeling, replacing the flat vocabulary distribution with a tree-structured factorization to achieve
logarithmic complexity in vocabulary size (Morin & Bengio, 2005; Mnih & Hinton, 2008). This
approach was later popularized in large-scale word embedding models (Mikolov et al., 2013) and
extended to neural machine translation and other large-vocabulary settings (Jean et al., 2015). Mi et
al. (Mi et al., 2016) introduce vocabulary shortlist pruning for neural machine translation, where a
small, input-dependent target vocabulary is constructed using lexical and alignment cues, allowing
decoding to avoid scoring the full vocabulary while largely preserving translation quality. More
recent variants, such as adaptive softmax, further exploit hierarchical structure to improve training
efficiency on modern hardware (Grave et al., 2017). However, these methods have primarily tar-
geted training efficiency or embedding learning, and have not been widely adopted to accelerate the
decode-time output projection in modern autoregressive large language models. In light of this hier-
archical embedding research, we must understand the structure of the embedding space of modern
LLMs. Prior work has shown that these spaces tend to be highlyanisotropic, meaning that variance
is concentrated in a few dominant directions rather than being evenly distributed. Mu et al. (2017)
showed that removing the top principal components of word embeddings improves semantic perfor-
mance, indicating that these directions encode shared, non-discriminative information. Ethayarajh
(2019) further demonstrated that contextual embeddings from models such as BERT and GPT-2
occupy narrow cones, with similarity dominated by common components rather than meaningful
structure. More recent work argues that such anisotropy is a fundamental property of neural repre-
sentations learned during training, rather than a simple artifact of optimization (Rudman & Eickhoff,
2024). These findings suggest that token embeddings do not form clean clusters, making centroid-
based grouping methods such as k-means less suitable. Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) finds
linear projections that maximize class separation while minimizing within-class variance (Fisher,
1936). Its discriminative objective remains useful in modern deep embedding learning (Wu et al.,
2016; Bartan & Pilanci, 2022) and pruning/efficient classification (Tian et al., 2017), suggesting
that Fisher-style projections are well-suited for constructing efficient decision boundaries in high-
dimensional neural embedding spaces.
3 METHODS
We design HiDRA as a lightweight modification to the LMHead of an existing language model.
Instead of scoring the full vocabulary with a dense projection, we construct a hierarchy of binary de-
cision vectors that progressively partition the token set. These decision vectors are initialized using
Fisher LDA projections derived from the token embeddings, and are then refined using supervised
training. At inference time, routing can terminate at any depth under beam routing, after which the
original LMHead scores only the tokens in the reached partitions.
LDA-based decision vectorsLete k ∈R d be the LMHead embedding for tokenkandh∈R d the
hidden state. Standard decoding computesarg max k h⊤ek at costO(V d). HiDRA arranges tokens
in a binary tree; each internal nodeℓpredictsbit ℓ =1[h ⊤dℓ +b ℓ >0]. Sincehis unknown at
construction time, we modelh=e t +ρwithρ∼ N(0,Σ), wheretis the true next token. Define the
marginm t :=d ⊤et +b. An error occurs whensign(d ⊤h+b)̸= sign(m t), i.e.d ⊤h+b=m t +d ⊤ρ
flips sign. Becaused ⊤ρ∼ N(0, d⊤Σd), a Gaussian tail bound yields

Optimal direction.For a node splitting tokens intoLvs.Rwith meansµ L, µR and within-class
covarianceΣ w, the expected margin scales withd ⊤(µR −µ L). Since the true noise covariance is
unknown, we approximate it using the within-class covarianceΣ w, which empirically aligns well
with the structure of LLM embedding spaces. Thus we solve the Fisher objective

decision direction is the LDA separator; we use these LDA vectors to initialize internal nodes.

Figure 1: HiDRA evaluation on Gemma 3 270M-IT (WildChat). (a) Perplexity increases with tree
depth. (b) Projection-only speedup, excluding routing overhead, grows exponentially with depth
and decreases with beam width. (c) Beam routing improves top-1 accuracy at fixed speedups.
Decision vector trainingWhile LDA provides a principled initialization, it ignores token fre-
quency and the true distribution of hidden states. We therefore fine-tune each decision vector using
teacher-forced hidden states, training a binary classifier at each node with a binary cross-entropy
loss. This adapts routing boundaries to real model activations observed on WildChat. For each node
ℓ, we train a binary classifier to predict the correct routing bit:
Lℓ =BCE( ˆbℓ, btrue
ℓ ).
Training is performed on model completions from the WildChat dataset, allowing the decision
boundaries to adapt to the true distribution of hidden states and token frequencies.
Hierarchical probability and early stoppingEach internal nodeℓoutputs a routing probability
pℓ =σ(h ⊤dℓ +b ℓ). For a tokenkwith path bits(b 1, . . . , bL), the induced hierarchical probability
factorizes as
p(k) =
LY
ℓ=1
p bℓ
ℓ (1−p ℓ)1−bℓ ,
which defines a valid distribution over the vocabulary via the tree structure. At inference time, rout-
ing may terminate early at depthl < L. In this case, the model evaluates the original LMHead only
over the tokens in the reached subtree, yielding a truncated distribution. This enables a continuous
speed–accuracy tradeoff by controlling the routing depth and beam width. Because early stopping
does not normalize over the full vocabulary, the resulting distribution differs from the base model
softmax. Consequently, perplexity values are not directly comparable to baseline perplexity and
should be interpreted only as a heuristic diagnostic of routing quality.
Beam routingGreedy routing restricts the candidate tokens to a single branch of the tree, which
may exclude high-probability tokens that lie across nearby partitions. To address this, we use beam
routing. At each level, the topkrouting paths are retained based on their cumulative probabilities.
The final candidate set is formed from the union of the tokens in these beam-selected partitions.
This allows the model to consider tokens from multiple regions of the embedding space, improving
accuracy while still providing substantial computational savings.
4 EXPERIMENTS
4.1 SETUP
We evaluate HiDRA onGemma 3 270M-IT(Team et al., 2025) usingWildChatprompt–
completion data (Zhao et al., 2024). The base language model is kept frozen; only the routing
tree is trained. We construct a depth-18 hierarchical bitmap tree over the Gemma vocabulary
(|V|= 262,144) using a Fisher LDA–motivated median-split procedure on the input embedding
matrix. This produces per-token path bitmaps and per-node split parameters. We then train the tree’s
decision vectors with next-token supervision on WildChat. Training uses sequence length 512, batch
size 16, for 5 epochs with AdamW (learning rate3×10 −4). We use a 90k/5k train/validation split,

only” column isolates the restricted LMHead computation after routing. The “Route-only” column
reports fused native CPU routing latency for the same depth/beam setting from the separate 8-thread
route-only benchmark. Baseline LMHead has no routing stage.
evaluating every 1000 steps. At inference, hidden states are routed to depthl, after which the origi-
nal LM head scores only tokens in the reached subtree. We report next-token top-1 accuracy relative
to the base model, perplexity computed from the hierarchical routing distribution, and projection-
only speed measured as milliseconds per token for the restricted LMHead computation after routing.
These timings exclude routing overhead and the base model forward pass. Projection speed is eval-
uated on CPU across depths0–17and beam widthsk∈ {1,2,4,8,16}using 100 warmup and 1000
timed iterations per setting.
4.2 RESULTS
Figure 1 summarizes the projection-speed–accuracy tradeoff of HiDRA across routing depths and
beam widths. Table 1 highlights representative operating points. At the representative operating
point(l= 4, k= 4)with 4 CPU threads, HiDRA reduces isolated output-stage latency from
15.33±0.04to1.91±0.02ms/token (8.04±0.09×), which translates into a teacher-forced full-step
decode reduction from61.08 to 49.11 ms/token (1.24×)because transformer forward time remains
dominant. We intentionally isolate the output projection in Figure 1(b) and Table 1 to expose the
scaling behavior of the LMHead itself; however, fused native CPU routing remains small in prac-
tice, staying below0.1ms/token across all depths and beam widths. Figure 1(a) shows perplexity
increasing monotonically with depth, largely independent of beam width, indicating that perplexity
is primarily controlled by the truncation depth rather than multi-path routing. Figure 1(b) shows that
projection-only speedup grows approximately exponentially with depth, while larger beam widths
reduce speed by increasing the number of candidate tokens that must be scored. Figure 1(c) demon-
strates that beam routing substantially recovers top-1 accuracy at fixed speedups. Additional anal-
yses appear in the appendix. Appendix A.1 summarizes teacher-forced decode across CPU thread
counts. Appendix A.3 shows that a WildChat-trained router retains a similar fraction of dense-model
top-1 accuracy on held-out WildChat and out-of-domain FineWeb-EDU.
5 CONCLUSION
We introduced HiDRA, a hierarchical decision routing layer that replaces dense full-vocabulary LM-
Head scoring with a sequence of binary routing decisions followed by restricted candidate scoring.
On Gemma, HiDRA provides substantial speedups while maintaining strong top-1 accuracy, and
beam routing further improves accuracy at fixed operating points. Because routing depth is cho-
sen at inference time, HiDRA offers a continuous spectrum of speed–quality tradeoffs that can be
adapted to hardware or latency constraints. HiDRA is mathematically grounded in an LDA formu-
lation and operates as a lightweight post-training modification that does not retrain the base model.
With a fused CPU router, routing overhead remains small relative to dense LMHead scoring, yield-
ing an8.04×speedup for the full output stage including routing at a representative operating point;
in teacher-forced autoregressive decoding, this translates into a practical1.24×end-to-end speedup
because transformer forward time remains dominant. Evaluations on held-out FineWeb-EDU fur-
ther indicate that a WildChat-trained router preserves a similar fraction of base-model accuracy out
of domain even when absolute task difficulty changes substantially. Overall, HiDRA shows that the
LMHead can be replaced with a hierarchical routing structure that yields real system-level gains
without modifying or retraining the underlying model.
